mainTopic: Fixing alleys open at both ends: whether a door is needed and must be locked, and whether one may combine the stringencies of רב and שמואל
overview: The גמרא asks how a ברייתא could speak of making an עירוב for a רשות הרבים. The חכמים told רבי יהודה that a public street cannot be fixed with a לחי or קורה, and teachings about ירושלים and מחוזא show that only actually locked doors help. So רב יהודה re-reads the ברייתא as being about alleys open at both ends (מבואות המפולשין): a צורת הפתח on one end and a לחי or קורה on the other. רב rules like the תנא קמא, while שמואל rules like חנניה, who requires a door on one end. The גמרא asks whether that door must be locked. שמואל rules it need not be, and the story of רב נחמן clearing the gates of נהרדעא shows the door only has to be able to close. Next, an L-shaped alleyway in נהרדעא was required to have doors by combining רב's stringency (the L-shape counts as open) with שמואל's (an open alley needs doors). The גמרא challenges this with a ברייתא that condemns taking the stringencies of both בית שמאי and בית הלל. It first resolves a contradiction inside that ברייתא's wording, and the discussion continues on the next amud.

steps.title: רבי יהודה's case of two houses across a public street
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא quotes רבי יהודה: a man with houses on both sides of a רשות הרבים may put up a לחי or a קורה on each side and then carry in the middle.
steps.simpleTranslation: If someone has two houses on the two sides of a public street, he puts a side post here and a side post there, or a crossbeam here and a crossbeam there, and then he may carry in the middle.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא is quoting a source (the view of רבי יהודה) as the first half of a challenge. It is setting up the next step, where the חכמים will reply.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבי יהודה holds that simple symbolic markers, a לחי or a קורה, at both ends of the street section between his houses are enough to turn it into a private area. This is very lenient, because the area is a real public street. The גמרא brings this case because the answer of the חכמים will matter for the ברייתא being discussed.

keyTerms.meaning: Public domain: a main public street where carrying on שבת is forbidden מן התורה
Side post: a thin upright post at the side of an alley's entrance
Crossbeam: a beam laid across the top of an alley's entrance
Literally 'carries and gives': he may move objects freely

steps.confusionAlert: This is not the conclusion. The גמרא brings רבי יהודה's view only so it can show that the חכמים reject it. The real point is the reply in the next step.

phrases.english: One who had two houses
phrases.notes: These are still רבי יהודה's words, carrying on from where he said 'יתר על כן' earlier.

phrases.english: on the two sides of the public domain,
places a side post here and a side post there,
phrases.notes: Placed at both ends of the street section between the houses.

phrases.english: or a crossbeam here and a crossbeam there,
and he may carry and place objects in the middle.

steps.triggerLanguage: מִי שֶׁהָיוּ לוֹ שְׁנֵי בָתִּים מִשְּׁנֵי צִידֵּי רְשׁוּת הָרַבִּים
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Opens the quoted source the גמרא uses to question the ברייתא of 'how to make an עירוב for a רשות הרבים' (earlier).
steps.mimraCoreRuling: According to רבי יהודה, a לחי or קורה on each side makes the part of a public street between one's two houses fit for carrying.

steps.title: The חכמים reply: a public domain cannot be fixed this way
steps.stepSummary: The חכמים tell רבי יהודה that a רשות הרבים cannot be made fit for carrying this way. This works as a challenge to the ברייתא that discusses making an עירוב for a public domain.
steps.simpleTranslation: They said to him: You cannot make an עירוב for a public domain this way.
steps.whatsHappening: The חכמים reject רבי יהודה's leniency. The גמרא uses their answer to attack the ברייתא that described how to make an עירוב for a רשות הרבים.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If a true public street cannot be fixed with a לחי or קורה, it looks like a רשות הרבים cannot get an עירוב at all. That clashes with the ברייתא, which plainly asked 'how do we make an עירוב for a רשות הרבים?' and gave an answer.

keyTerms.meaning: Make fit for carrying (through an עירוב or symbolic partitions)
In this manner (with a לחי or קורה)

phrases.english: They said to him: One cannot render fit for carrying
a public domain in this manner.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמְרוּ לוֹ: אֵין מְעָרְבִין רְשׁוּת הָרַבִּים בְּכָךְ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Completes the quoted source: the חכמים reject the view in step 1, and that rejection is the core of the challenge.
steps.kashyaTarget: The ברייתא that teaches how to make an עירוב for a רשות הרבים.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The חכמים say a public domain cannot be fixed with a לחי or קורה. So how can the ברייתא speak of making an עירוב for a public domain at all?

steps.title: Even doors do not help unless they are locked: the case of ירושלים
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא blocks a possible escape. Maybe doors would work where a לחי or קורה does not? No. רבי יוחנן teaches that ירושלים would be a רשות הרבים if its doors were not actually locked at night.
steps.simpleTranslation: And if you say that only this way (with a לחי or קורה) a public domain cannot be fixed, but with doors it can, didn't רבה בר בר חנה say in the name of רבי יוחנן: ירושלים, if not for the fact that its doors are locked at night, one would be liable for carrying in it as a public domain!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא expects someone to say 'only a לחי or קורה fails, but doors would succeed.' It rejects this with רבי יוחנן's teaching about ירושלים.
steps.deeperAnalysis: ירושלים had gates, but רבי יוחנן says only the fact that they were locked kept it from being a רשות הרבים. So having doors is not enough; they must actually be closed. That makes the challenge stronger: none of the methods mentioned in the ברייתא (which does not require locking) could fix a true public domain.

keyTerms.meaning: And if you will say: introduces a possible answer that the גמרא is about to reject

steps.confusionAlert: The proof is about doors that are actually locked, not doors that merely exist. A door that stands open does not stop the area from being a רשות הרבים.

phrases.english: And if you say that in this manner
it is what cannot be rendered fit,
phrases.notes: He means it can't be made fit with only a לחי or קורה.

phrases.english: but with doors it can be rendered fit,
but didn't Rabba bar bar Ḥana say
that Rabbi Yoḥanan said:
Jerusalem, were it not that its doors
are locked at night,
one would be liable for carrying in it as a public domain!

steps.triggerLanguage: וְכִי תֵּימָא בְּכָךְ הוּא דְּלָא מִיעָרְבָא, הָא בִּדְלָתוֹת מִיעָרְבָא, וְהָאָמַר
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Strengthens the challenge of step 2 by closing off the 'doors would work' escape.
steps.kashyaTarget: The possible defense that doors could fix a רשות הרבים.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: ירושלים had doors, yet only the actual locking stopped it from being a רשות הרבים. So unlocked doors do not help, and the ברייתא's methods cannot fix a true public domain.

steps.title: עולא adds: the city gates of מחוזא
steps.stepSummary: עולא gives a second, similar teaching: the gates of מחוזא would make them a רשות הרבים if their doors were not actually locked.
steps.simpleTranslation: And עולא said: These gateways of מחוזא, if not for the fact that their doors are locked, one would be liable for carrying in them as a public domain.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a second source that says the same thing as רבי יוחנן, to back up the point.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Now two אמוראים agree: a public area stays a רשות הרבים unless real doors are actually locked. This sets the stage for the problem the next step must solve: the ברייתא cannot be talking about a true public domain.

keyTerms.meaning: מחוזא, a large Babylonian trading city on the Tigris

phrases.english: And Ulla said:
These city entrances of Meḥoza,
were it not that their doors are locked,
one would be liable for carrying in them as a public domain.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Adds a second source supporting step 3.
steps.raayaObject: The claim that only actually locked doors stop an area from being a רשות הרבים.
steps.raayaSupportSource: עולא's teaching about the gateways of מחוזא.

steps.title: רב יהודה re-reads the ברייתא as being about open-ended alleys
steps.stepSummary: רב יהודה says the ברייתא was never about a true רשות הרבים. It means alleys that are open at both ends onto the public domain, and these are fixed with a צורת הפתח on one end and a לחי or קורה on the other.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב יהודה said, this is what the ברייתא means: How do we make an עירוב for alleys that open at both ends onto a public domain? One makes a doorway-frame on one side and a side post or crossbeam on the other side.
steps.whatsHappening: רב יהודה answers the challenge by re-reading the words of the ברייתא. It is about מבואות המפולשין (alleys open at both ends), not about a real public street.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A true רשות הרבים needs locked doors, but an alley open at both ends is not itself a public domain. It only needs symbolic closure: a צורת הפתח on one side and a לחי or קורה on the other. This removes the contradiction with the חכמים, רבי יוחנן, and עולא.

keyTerms.meaning: This is what it means: introduces a re-reading of a text
Alleys open at both ends (running from one public area to another)
Form of a doorway: two posts with a beam or string across the top

steps.whatToRemember: A true רשות הרבים cannot be fixed by a לחי, a קורה, or even unlocked doors; only actually locked doors help. The ברייתא's 'עירוב for a public domain' really means alleys open at both ends (מבואות המפולשין), fixed with a צורת הפתח on one side and a לחי or קורה on the other.
steps.confusionAlert: The words 'לחי וקורה' here mean a לחי OR a קורה on the second side. You do not need both.
steps.whyThisMatters: This sets the basic rule for alleys open at both ends: one side needs a real doorway-form and the other side needs only a minimal marker. The rest of the sugya builds on this distinction.

phrases.english: Rav Yehuda said: This is what it is saying:
How does one render alleyways fit for carrying
that are open at both ends into the public domain?
He makes a form of a doorway on one side,
and a side post or a crossbeam on the other side.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Resolves the challenge built up in steps 2 through 4 by re-reading the ברייתא.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Re-reading the ברייתא's case: it is about open-ended alleys, not a true public domain.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The ברייתא seemed to describe making an עירוב for an actual רשות הרבים.
steps.terutzMaskana: The ברייתא refers to מבואות המפולשין, which are fixed with a צורת הפתח on one side and a לחי or קורה on the other. A true רשות הרבים still needs actually locked doors.

steps.title: רב and שמואל disagree on whose view is the הלכה
steps.stepSummary: רב rules like the תנא קמא of the ברייתא. שמואל rules like חנניה, who follows בית הלל and requires a door on one end.
steps.simpleTranslation: It was stated: רב said the הלכה follows the first תנא. שמואל said the הלכה follows חנניה.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא reports a disagreement between two אמוראים about which opinion in the ברייתא we follow in practice.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The תנא קמא says an alley open at both ends needs only a צורת הפתח on one end and a לחי or קורה on the other. חנניה, explaining בית הלל, says one end must have an actual door. רב follows the easier view. שמואל follows the stricter view that requires a door.

keyTerms.meaning: The first, unnamed תנא in a ברייתא or משנה
The practical ruling, meaning the opinion we actually follow

steps.confusionAlert: Don't mix up the two sides. רב's view (the תנא קמא) never requires a door. Only שמואל's view (חנניה) requires a door. Everything that follows about locking the door only applies to שמואל's side.
steps.whyThisMatters: שמואל requires a door, so the next question follows naturally: does that door have to actually be locked?

phrases.english: It was stated:
Rav said: The halacha is like the first tanna.
phrases.notes: A צורת הפתח on one end and a לחי or קורה on the other is enough.

phrases.english: And Shmuel said: The halacha is like Chananya.
phrases.notes: חנניה is following בית הלל here: a door on one end.

steps.triggerLanguage: אִיתְּמַר. רַב אָמַר: הִילְכְתָא כְּתַנָּא קַמָּא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: רב יהודה explained that the ברייתא is about alleys open at both ends. Now the אמוראים rule which view in that ברייתא is the הלכה.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: רב: the הלכה follows the תנא קמא (no door needed). שמואל: the הלכה follows חנניה (a door is needed on one end).

steps.title: Must the door actually be locked according to חנניה?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks whether the door that חנניה requires must really be locked, or only needs to be there.
steps.simpleTranslation: They asked: according to חנניה, who follows בית הלל, does the door need to be locked, or does it not need to be locked?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא raises a real question about the details of חנניה's view. It is setting up the answers that come next.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Earlier, רבי יוחנן and עולא taught that city gates only stop a place from being a רשות הרבים if they are actually locked. That raises the question here: is a door that can close enough, or must it actually be locked?

keyTerms.meaning: They asked. This introduces a real question that needs an answer.

phrases.english: They asked:
According to Chananya, in the view of Beit Hillel,

phrases.aramaic: צָרִיךְ לִנְעוֹל, אוֹ אֵין צָרִיךְ לִנְעוֹל?
phrases.english: must it be locked, or need it not be locked?

steps.triggerLanguage: אִיבַּעְיָא לְהוּ: לַחֲנַנְיָה אַלִּיבָּא דְּבֵית הִלֵּל
steps.relationToPreviousStep: After hearing that שמואל rules like חנניה, the גמרא asks a detail of that view.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Whether the door חנניה requires must actually be locked.

steps.title: שמואל rules that the door need not be locked
steps.stepSummary: Two students, רב יהודה and רב מתנה, report in שמואל's name that the door need not be locked. Another version says רב מתנה had a real case and שמואל ruled that way for him.
steps.simpleTranslation: Come and hear: רב יהודה said in שמואל's name, it need not be locked. רב מתנה also said in שמואל's name, it need not be locked. Some say רב מתנה said: this happened to me, and שמואל told me it need not be locked.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the question by quoting שמואל, who said no locking is needed.
steps.deeperAnalysis: שמואל is the one who rules like חנניה, so his opinion on the detail settles it. The second version makes the answer stronger. It is not only a teaching but a real-life ruling (מעשה רב) given to רב מתנה.

keyTerms.meaning: It happened to me myself. This is a real case.

phrases.english: Come and hear,
for Rav Yehuda said that Shmuel said:
It need not be locked.

phrases.aramaic: וְכֵן אָמַר רַב מַתְנָה אָמַר שְׁמוּאֵל:
phrases.english: And similarly Rav Mattana said that Shmuel said:
It need not be locked.
Some say that Rav Mattana said:
A case happened to me myself,

phrases.aramaic: וְאָמַר לִי שְׁמוּאֵל: אֵין צָרִיךְ לִנְעוֹל.
phrases.english: and Shmuel said to me: It need not be locked.

steps.triggerLanguage: תָּא שְׁמַע, דְּאָמַר רַב יְהוּדָה אָמַר שְׁמוּאֵל
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Directly answers the question of step 7.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: According to שמואל, the door does not need to be locked.

steps.title: The same question is put to רב ענן
steps.stepSummary: People ask רב ענן whether the door must be locked.
steps.simpleTranslation: They asked רב ענן: does it need to be locked, or does it not need to be locked?
steps.whatsHappening: The same question is asked again, this time directly to רב ענן. This sets up his answer in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Nothing new is added to the question itself. What is new is who is being asked. רב ענן answers by pointing to something he saw שמואל do.

keyTerms.meaning: They asked of him. This introduces a question put to a specific sage.

phrases.english: They asked Rav Anan:

phrases.aramaic: צָרִיךְ לִנְעוֹל אוֹ אֵין צָרִיךְ לִנְעוֹל?
phrases.english: Must it be locked or need it not be locked?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Repeats the locking question to a new sage.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Whether the door must actually be locked.

steps.title: Proof from the half-buried gates of נהרדעא
steps.stepSummary: רב ענן points to the gates of נהרדעא. They were half-buried in earth and could not be closed, yet שמואל walked through them and never complained.
steps.simpleTranslation: He said to them: Come and see these gates of נהרדעא. They are buried up to half their height in earth. מר שמואל goes in and out through them, and he never said anything to the people about them.
steps.whatsHappening: רב ענן proves from what שמואל did (and did not say) that the door does not need to be locked.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Doors buried halfway in dirt cannot possibly be closed or locked. If locking were required, שמואל would have told the people to fix it. His silence shows he holds that locking is not needed.

keyTerms.meaning: Come and see. This introduces a proof from something seen.
נהרדעא, the city of שמואל in Babylonia
That are buried or filled in

phrases.english: He said to them: Come and see
these gates of Neharde'a
which are buried up to half their height in earth,
and Mar Shmuel goes in and out,
and he did not say anything at all to them.

steps.triggerLanguage: אֲמַר לְהוּ: תָּא חֲזִי הָנֵי אֲבוּלֵּי דִּנְהַרְדָּעָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers רב ענן's question with a proof from שמואל's behavior.
steps.raayaObject: That the door does not need to be locked.
steps.raayaSupportSource: שמואל's silence about the gates of נהרדעא, which could not be closed.

steps.title: רב כהנא: those gates were blocked, so they prove nothing
steps.stepSummary: רב כהנא rejects the proof. The gates of נהרדעא were blocked, so they are a special case.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב כהנא said: Those gates were blocked.
steps.whatsHappening: רב כהנא pushes away רב ענן's proof by showing that the gates of נהרדעא were different from an ordinary open door.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The earth filling the gates partly sealed them, so they did not need locking. That tells us nothing about a regular door that stands open. So the proof from שמואל's silence falls away.
steps.whatToRemember: שמואל rules like חנניה: an alley open at both ends needs a door on one end. Reports in שמואל's name say the door need not be locked. But רב ענן's proof from the gates of נהרדעא is rejected by רב כהנא, because those gates were blocked.
steps.confusionAlert: רב כהנא does not quote anyone who disagrees with שמואל. He only says the נהרדעא case cannot serve as proof, because blocked gates are a different situation from a normal open door.

phrases.english: Rav Kahana said:
Those were blocked.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַב כָּהֲנָא: הָנָךְ מְגוּפוֹת הֲוַאי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Rejects the proof brought in step 10.
steps.dechiyaRejectionScope: Rejects only רב ענן's proof from נהרדעא. It does not argue against the reports quoted in step 8.
steps.dechiyaFlawIdentified: The gates were blocked with earth, so they are not like an ordinary door, and nothing can be learned from them about whether a door must be locked.

steps.title: רב נחמן orders the earth cleared from the gates
steps.stepSummary: When רב נחמן came to נהרדעא, he ordered that the earth piled against the gates be cleared away.
steps.simpleTranslation: When רב נחמן came, he said: Clear away their earth.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא continues the story of the half-buried gates of נהרדעא. רב נחמן ordered the earth removed so the doors could move again.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רב כהנא had just said the gates were a special case because they were blocked. Now רב נחמן actually fixes them by clearing the dirt. This makes it look like the doors had to be usable for the alleyway to work.

keyTerms.meaning: Their earth, the dirt piled against them

phrases.english: When Rav Nachman came, he said:
Clear away their earth.
phrases.notes: The dirt that had buried the gates of נהרדעא

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues the story of the נהרדעא gates after רב כהנא's rejection
steps.mimraCoreRuling: רב נחמן had the earth cleared from the gates so the doors could function.

steps.title: Does רב נחמן hold the door must be locked?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא suggests that רב נחמן's order shows he holds the door must actually be locked.
steps.simpleTranslation: Shall we say that רב נחמן holds that one must lock the door?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא tries to learn a rule from רב נחמן's action. Maybe he cleared the dirt because he holds the doors must really be shut.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Why else would he bother clearing the earth? The גמרא proposes that he must hold the strict side of the question raised in Step 7, that the door has to be actually locked.

keyTerms.meaning: Shall we say (introduces a suggested inference)

phrases.english: Shall we say that Rav Nachman holds:
One must lock the door?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Tries to infer רב נחמן's position from his action in Step 12
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Does רב נחמן's clearing of the earth show that he requires the door to be actually locked?

steps.title: The doors only need to be able to lock
steps.stepSummary: No. The doors only need to be fit to lock, even if nobody actually locks them.
steps.simpleTranslation: No. Since they are fit to be locked, it is enough, even though they are not actually locked.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא rejects the suggestion from Step 13. רב נחמן only wanted the doors to be able to close.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Buried doors cannot close at all, so they fail even the easier requirement. Clearing the dirt makes them closable. That does not prove they must actually be locked, so רב נחמן can agree with שמואל from Step 8.
steps.confusionAlert: Do not mix up 'fit to lock' with 'locked.' The buried gates of נהרדעא failed because they could not close at all. Clearing them is enough even if they stay open.

phrases.english: No, since they are fit to be locked,
it is enough, even though they are not actually locked.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Rejects the inference proposed in Step 13
steps.dechiyaRejectionScope: Rejects only the inference about רב נחמן, not the requirement of a door
steps.dechiyaFlawIdentified: Clearing the earth can be explained by the need for the doors to be able to close, not to be locked
steps.whatToRemember: The door must be able to lock. It does not have to be actually locked.

steps.title: An L-shaped alleyway in נהרדעא needed doors
steps.stepSummary: For an L-shaped alleyway in נהרדעא, the rabbis applied both רב's stringency and שמואל's stringency and required doors.
steps.simpleTranslation: There was a certain L-shaped alleyway in נהרדעא. They placed on it the stringency of רב and the stringency of שמואל, and required doors for it.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא tells a new story about a bent alleyway. This sets up the next steps, where the גמרא explains which stringency came from each אמורא.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A מבוי עקום bends in an L-shape. Here the rulers combined one strict view of רב with one strict view of שמואל. Together these led to the demand for real doors.

phrases.english: A certain bent alleyway
that was in Nehardea,
they placed upon it the stringency of Rav
and the stringency of Shmuel,
and required it to have doors.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Opens a new case about an L-shaped alleyway
steps.mimraCoreRuling: An L-shaped alleyway in נהרדעא was required to have doors, based on stringencies of both רב and שמואל.

steps.title: רב's stringency: the L-shape counts as open
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא proposes that רב's stringency is his view that an L-shaped alleyway is treated like an alleyway open at both ends.
steps.simpleTranslation: The stringency of רב: he said its law is like an alleyway open at both ends.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא starts to explain the story. It names the first stringency it thinks came from רב.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רב treats the bend as if the alleyway runs straight through, open on both ends. That is strict, because an open alleyway needs more than a simple post or beam.

keyTerms.meaning: Its law, how it is treated

phrases.english: The stringency of Rav, who said: its law is like an alleyway open at both ends.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Explains the first stringency mentioned in Step 15
steps.mimraCoreRuling: רב holds an L-shaped alleyway is treated like an alleyway open at both ends.

steps.title: But רב rules leniently on open alleyways
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא objects. רב ruled like the תנא קמא, who does not require doors even for an open alleyway.
steps.simpleTranslation: But did רב not say the law follows the תנא קמא?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges Step 16. If you follow רב, you would never end up needing doors.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The תנא קמא says an open alleyway only needs a צורת הפתח on one end and a לחי or קורה on the other (step 5), never an actual door. So even if the L-shape counts as open, רב himself would not demand doors. Something else must be the source of the door requirement.

keyTerms.meaning: But did he not say (introduces a challenge)
The first, unnamed תנא of the ברייתא

phrases.english: But didn't Rav say the law follows the first Tanna?!
phrases.notes: The תנא קמא requires only a doorway-frame, not doors

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the attribution in Step 16
steps.kashyaTarget: The claim that the door requirement comes from רב
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: רב follows the תנא קמא, who never requires doors, so רב cannot be the source of the door requirement

steps.title: The doors come from שמואל, who follows חנניה
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא answers that the door requirement comes from שמואל, who rules like חנניה.
steps.simpleTranslation: They followed שמואל, who said the law follows חנניה.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers Step 17. The door requirement comes from שמואל, not רב.
steps.deeperAnalysis: חנניה holds that an open alleyway needs a door. שמואל rules like חנניה, so the doors are שמואל's stringency.

phrases.english: Like Shmuel, who said: the law follows Chananya.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers Step 17 by moving the door requirement to שמואל
steps.terutzMaskana: The doors came from שמואל, who rules like חנניה

steps.title: But שמואל treats the L-shape as closed
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא objects again. שמואל holds an L-shaped alleyway is like a closed one, which needs no doors.
steps.simpleTranslation: But did שמואל not say its law is like a closed alleyway?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges Step 18. By שמואל's own view, this alleyway would not need doors.
steps.deeperAnalysis: According to שמואל, the bend makes the alleyway count as closed on one side. A closed alleyway never needs doors. So שמואל alone cannot explain the ruling either.

phrases.english: But didn't Shmuel say its law is like a closed alleyway!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the answer of Step 18
steps.kashyaTarget: The claim that the doors follow שמואל
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: שמואל treats an L-shaped alleyway as closed, and a closed alleyway never needs doors

steps.title: Combining רב on the L-shape with שמואל on doors
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא answers that on the L-shape they followed רב, who treats it as open. Combined with שמואל's demand for doors on open alleyways, doors were required.
steps.simpleTranslation: They followed רב, who said its law is like an open alleyway.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא finishes explaining the ruling. Each אמורא supplied one strict piece, and together they require doors.
steps.deeperAnalysis: From רב they took 'the L-shape counts as open.' From שמואל they took 'an open alleyway needs doors.' Neither אמורא alone would require doors, but the combination does.

keyTerms.meaning: רב's stringency: the L-shape counts as open
שמואל's stringency: an open alleyway needs doors

steps.confusionAlert: Each אמורא is strict on one point and lenient on the other. רב: the L-shape is open (strict), but an open alleyway needs no doors (lenient). שמואל: the L-shape is closed (lenient), but an open alleyway needs doors (strict). The ruling took only the strict half from each.
steps.whatToRemember: The נהרדעא ruling took רב's stringency on the L-shape and שמואל's stringency on doors.

phrases.english: Like Rav, who said its law is like an open alleyway.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers Step 19 by splitting the two issues between רב and שמואל
steps.terutzResolutionType: Splitting the case into two separate issues
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The whole ruling must follow a single Amora
steps.terutzMaskana: The L-shape question follows רב, and the door question follows שמואל

steps.title: May one combine the stringencies of two opposing views?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא challenges the idea of taking stringencies from two disputing authorities. It quotes a ברייתא that calls one who takes both sides' stringencies a fool.
steps.simpleTranslation: But do we act according to two stringencies? It was taught in a ברייתא: The law always follows בית הלל. One who wants to act like בית שמאי may do so, and one who wants to act like בית הלל may do so. One who takes the leniencies of בית שמאי and the leniencies of בית הלל is wicked. About one who takes the stringencies of בית שמאי and the stringencies of בית הלל, the verse says: 'The fool walks in darkness.' Rather, follow either בית שמאי in their leniencies and stringencies, or בית הלל in their leniencies and stringencies.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא attacks the method used in Step 20. A ברייתא says you may not mix two opposing opinions' stringencies.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The ברייתא says you must stay consistent with one school, both its strict and its lenient rulings. Taking only the strict side of each is called foolish. That is exactly what the נהרדעא ruling did with רב and שמואל, so it looks wrong. Before answering, the גמרא deals with a side problem in this ברייתא's own wording (steps 22–24). The answer to this main challenge comes on the next amud.

keyTerms.meaning: But it was taught in a ברייתא
The fool walks in darkness (קהלת ב:יד)

steps.whyThisMatters: This ברייתא is a key source for the rule against mixing opposing positions, often called 'תרתי דסתרי.' Its principle reaches far beyond עירובין.

phrases.english: But do we act according to two stringencies?

phrases.aramaic: וְהָא תַּנְיָא: לְעוֹלָם הֲלָכָה כְּבֵית הִלֵּל,
phrases.english: But it was taught: The law always follows Beit Hillel,

phrases.aramaic: וְהָרוֹצֶה לַעֲשׂוֹת כְּדִבְרֵי בֵּית שַׁמַּאי עוֹשֶׂה,
phrases.english: and one who wants to act like Beit Shammai may do so,
and one who wants to act like Beit Hillel may do so.

phrases.aramaic: מִקּוּלֵּי בֵּית שַׁמַּאי וּמִקּוּלֵּי בֵּית הִלֵּל — רָשָׁע.
phrases.english: One who takes the leniencies of Beit Shammai and the leniencies of Beit Hillel is wicked.

phrases.aramaic: מֵחוּמְרֵי בֵּית שַׁמַּאי וּמֵחוּמְרֵי בֵּית הִלֵּל —
phrases.english: One who takes the stringencies of Beit Shammai and the stringencies of Beit Hillel,
about him the verse says:
"The fool walks in darkness."
Rather, either like Beit Shammai,
in their leniencies and in their stringencies,
or like Beit Hillel,
in their leniencies and in their stringencies.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the method of combining stringencies explained in Step 20
steps.kashyaTarget: The נהרדעא practice of combining רב's and שמואל's stringencies
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: A ברייתא calls one who adopts the stringencies of both disputing schools a fool, so combining רב's and שמואל's stringencies should be forbidden

steps.title: The ברייתא seems to contradict itself
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא points out that the ברייתא first rules that the הלכה is always like בית הלל, and then allows a person to follow בית שמאי.
steps.simpleTranslation: This ברייתא itself is difficult. You said the הלכה is always like בית הלל, and then you turned around and said that whoever wants to act like בית שמאי may do so?!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא steps aside from its main argument to point out a contradiction between two lines of the same ברייתא it quoted in step 21.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The first line, 'always like בית הלל', sounds like a binding rule. The next line lets a person freely choose בית שמאי. If the rule is 'always', there should be no room for that choice.

keyTerms.meaning: This itself is difficult. A source has an internal problem of its own.
And then you went back and said

steps.confusionAlert: This is a side question about the wording of the ברייתא. The גמרא has not yet answered the main challenge from step 21 about taking both stringencies.

phrases.english: This itself is difficult.
phrases.notes: Refers to the ברייתא quoted in step 21.

phrases.english: You said: the halakha is always like Beit Hillel,
and then you went back and said:

phrases.aramaic: הָרוֹצֶה לַעֲשׂוֹת כְּדִבְרֵי בֵּית שַׁמַּאי עוֹשֶׂה?!
phrases.english: one who wishes to act like the words of Beit Shammai may do so?!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Turns to an internal problem in the ברייתא cited in step 21, before continuing the main argument.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Internal contradiction: 'the הלכה is always like בית הלל' cannot fit with 'one may act like בית שמאי'.

steps.title: One line is from before the בת קול and one from after
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא answers that the line allowing a choice was taught before the בת קול ruled like בית הלל, and the 'always like בית הלל' line was taught after it.
steps.simpleTranslation: It is not difficult. Here, the line allowing a choice was said before the בת קול. Here, the line saying 'always like בית הלל' was said after the בת קול.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא resolves the contradiction by saying the two lines describe two different time periods.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Before the heavenly voice announced that the הלכה follows בית הלל, the question was still open, so a person could follow either school. After the בת קול, the הלכה was fixed as 'always like בית הלל'. So the two lines do not clash. They describe the situation before and after.

keyTerms.meaning: It is not difficult. This is the standard opening of an answer.
Here... here. Each statement applies to a different case.
A heavenly voice. Here it is the one that declared the הלכה like בית הלל.

steps.confusionAlert: Watch which line goes with which time. The freedom to follow בית שמאי is BEFORE the בת קול. 'Always like בית הלל' is AFTER the בת קול.

phrases.english: It is not difficult:
here — before the Divine Voice.
phrases.notes: The line allowing a person to follow בית שמאי.

phrases.english: here — after the Divine Voice.
phrases.notes: The line saying the הלכה is always like בית הלל.

steps.triggerLanguage: לָא קַשְׁיָא: כָּאן — קוֹדֶם בַּת קוֹל
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the internal contradiction raised in step 22.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Splitting by time period: the two lines are taught for before and after the בת קול.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Both lines seemed to describe the same moment, so they contradicted each other.
steps.terutzMaskana: The freedom to choose applied before the בת קול. After it, the הלכה is always like בית הלל.

steps.title: A second answer: both lines are from after the בת קול
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא begins an alternative answer: both lines of the ברייתא were said after the בת קול. The explanation continues in the next part of the text.
steps.simpleTranslation: And if you want, say a different answer: both this line and that line were said after the בת קול,
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא is setting up a second way to solve the contradiction. Here it only gives the opening claim, and the explanation of how this works comes next.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This answer refuses to split the lines by time, so both lines apply after the בת קול. That raises an obvious question: how can someone still follow בית שמאי after the heavenly ruling? The גמרא will need to explain this in the continuation.

keyTerms.meaning: And if you wish, say. This introduces an alternative answer.

phrases.english: And if you wish, say:
this and that — after the Divine Voice,
phrases.notes: The sentence continues on the next amud.

steps.triggerLanguage: וְאִיבָּעֵית אֵימָא: הָא וְהָא — לְאַחַר בַּת קוֹל
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Offers a second answer to step 22 that rejects step 23's time split.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Alternative answer, still in progress: both lines are from the same period, after the בת קול.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Step 23 assumed the lines must come from different times.
steps.terutzMaskana: Both lines apply after the בת קול. The reason this is possible is explained in the continuation.
